lifeplan / every combination of five conditions / example

1,176 ways this household could go

Five conditions were given two to seven options each, and every combination of those options was run as a complete life plan carried to the year the earner turns 100. The final net worth ranges from −1.78 to +4.43 hundred-million yen. The point of running them all is to see which condition moves the result. The household is invented; see the note at the end.

1,176combinations, each one run as a complete plan
50%of the spread comes from 経済, the condition with the most influence
94.7%of the spread is explained by the five conditions acting separately
160combinations had to turn the home into cash

What was varied

One condition per row. The first option of each condition is what the original plan assumed.

A scenario like "carry on as now" changes several things at once. A results row for it can only say which scenario was chosen, not which of its parts made the difference. Splitting the scenarios into separate conditions, each with a few options, and running every combination of options is what answers that question.

Nothing about this depends on the household. Any life plan is a set of decisions made under conditions nobody controls. Write each decision and each outside condition as a short list of options, run the plan once per combination, and the results show which decision is worth deliberating over and which is not. A single simulator run says only whether one particular plan works; this says what changes the answer.

How widely the results spread

Net worth in the final year, in today's prices, in hundred-million yen

In the simulator, assets stop at zero and never go negative. A plan that cannot pay a bill records the unpaid amount as a shortfall and keeps going. If the chart used assets alone, every ruined combination would sit at zero and the chart would go flat exactly where the differences matter most. So the measure used here is assets minus the accumulated shortfall, which can go below zero.

Which condition moves the result

Share of the spread each condition accounts for (variance explained, η²)

η² is the share of the total spread that disappears if one condition is held fixed. If the five shares added up to 100%, each condition would act on its own; whatever is missing is the part where conditions act together. Because every option of every condition appears in the same number of combinations, the spread can be split cleanly by condition. This is a more reliable measure of sensitivity than moving one factor at a time, because a one-at-a-time result depends on where the other factors happened to be parked.

The economy is not a choice

For each economy, every combination of the other four conditions

In the harshest economy (ゼロ成長枯渇), 87.5% of combinations fail. Only the most favourable settings of the household's decisions survive there. This is the sweep's most useful output: it shows how much of the problem is outside what the household can choose.

Each decision on its own

Median net worth and ruin rate for each option, across every combination of the other conditions

Where the rows of a table barely differ, that decision barely matters for this household: 年金受給開始 accounts for under 1% of the spread. That is a result too. It says which questions the household can stop deliberating over, and which one (住まい) deserves the time.

Housing and living cost together

Each row covers every combination of the other three conditions

The home is the last resource

When a plan cannot pay, it either sells the home and rents, or borrows against it

Both measures require the mortgage to be repaid first. A home already pledged cannot be pledged again, and selling means clearing the loan out of the proceeds. The plan evaluates both and takes whichever leaves the household better off.

What this sweep does not answer

How likely ruin is. 630 of the 1,176 combinations fail, which is 53.6%. That figure is the share of the options that were fed in, not a probability. Load the sweep with pessimistic economies and it rises; load it with optimistic ones and it falls. Turning it into a chance would require weighting each option by how likely it is, and nobody can do that accurately. The seven economies and the seven crash timings are counted equally here, and they are not equally likely. Read which condition moves the result, not how many combinations fail.

Asset allocation by age. Contributions follow one fixed policy, and nothing here varies the mix of shares and bonds. Knowing that a crash hurts most just before drawdown does not say what to do about it.

Care, job loss, inheritance. None of these was varied.

Anything about a real household. Every figure describes an invented one.

Doing the same for your own household

The simulator and the sweep are in the repository, and nothing in them is specific to this household. Three things change:

  1. Describe the household. Income, spending, housing, loans, pension and so on are one TSV file each under data/controllable/; the manifest projects/base.tsv lists which file fills which slot. Replace the figures with your own. The README in that directory says where each of the example figures came from.
  2. Write the options. Each option is another TSV file for the same slot; the ones used here are under data/controllable/scenario/ (decisions) and data/environment/scenario/ (economies, crashes).
  3. List the conditions. Axes() in tools/sweep/main.go names each condition, its options, and which file each option swaps in. Add, remove or rename conditions there. The number of plans to run is the product of the option counts.

Then run the three commands in the footer. The sweep runs one plan per combination on every core; the two scripts produce this page from the results.

Generated by tools/sweep, which passes overrides to plan.Build instead of writing 1,176 manifests. Results are in out/sweep/cells.tsv. Reproduce with go run ./tools/sweep && python3 examples/analyse.py && python3 examples/build.py.

The household in this report does not exist. Nobody lives on exactly these figures, but each figure comes from a published statistic. The salary comes from the 民間給与実態統計調査 by age band, the spouse's pay from the 賃金構造基本統計調査 hourly rate for part-time women, the spending from the 家計調査 for the head's age band, and the rent and purchase price from the going rate for a 70㎡ flat in 八王子市. Each source is cited in data/controllable/README.md. Only the household's makeup is invented; the decisions, the statutory rules and the economic projections are real. All amounts are in real terms, discounted to the plan's first year. Pension levels follow the 2024 財政検証. The crash size is a round figure chosen by hand rather than derived from any particular portfolio.
